CANADIAN

DECISION ON PRE-TRIAL APPLICATION
B
[1]

Section 278.3

of the
Criminal
Code

_______________________________________________________________________

The
proceedings in this case, including these reasons, are subject to an order made
under
s. 486
of the
Criminal Code
prohibiting the disclosure or
broadcast of any information that could disclose the identity of the
complainant or witness.

In
accordance with
section 278.9(1)
of the
Criminal Code
, it is prohibited
to publish or disseminate in any way the content of the request made pursuant
to
section 278.3
of the
Criminal Code
and anything that has been
presented as evidence during the hearing held in camera pursuant to
section
278.4
of the
Criminal Code
.
[2]

[
1
]

The accused is facing two charges, regarding sexual offences allegedly
committed in 1997 towards a person under the age of fourteen. The trial is set
to start today, June 17
th
, 2024.

[
2
]

The accused seeks to obtain access to the entire record of
third-party record holder,
Canadian Jewish News
(hereinafter
CJN
)
regarding an interview given by the complainant to one of its journalists,
Ellin Bessner.

[
3
]

More specifically, the complainant, participates to a Podcast
[3]
, published at the same time as
a news article, about the accused facing these criminal charges. The Podcast
and article both refer to past events pertaining to the accused that would have
been investigated by the Jewish Community Council of Montreal, leading to the
accused’s removal from the Community.

[
4
]

The accused files the articles dated [...],
2022, by Ellin Bessner, and the Podcast in question, to support his
application. Also tendered into evidence are the transcripts of the preliminary
inquiry, an article published by
CBC
on June 15, 2022, relating
to the charges laid against the accused, and email exchanges between the
complainant and Detective Harvey, the investigative officer in the present case.

[
5
]

The Podcast and news articles from
CJN
all refer to
the complainant being the person interviewed. However, the voice of the person
being interviewed is blurred and no images of this person are published. Also,
the identity of this person is never disclosed, and it is mentioned, more than
once, that there is a Court ordered publication ban prohibiting such disclosure.
Finally, in the Podcast, the journalist specifies that
CJN
has
protected the identity of the person being interviewed.

[
6
]

As for the other participants to the news articles and Podcast, they
are identified by names, titles in their profession, but also pictures of them.

[
7
]

Written observations from counsels for the complainant,
for the Crown

and for
CJN
are also filed.
[4]

[
8
]

Section 278.3 creates a regime governing the access to third-party held
records related to a complainant.

[
9
]

In a s. 278.3 third-party record application, the third-party record
holder and the person affected by the record (here, the complainant), are
parties to the application. Section 278.3(5) requires that they must receive
notice of, and be served with, the application. Section 278.4(2) provides them
with the right to appear and make submissions at the hearing and it removes
their compellability as witnesses.

[
10
]

CJN
, the
third-party record holder, was served and counsel appeared on its behalf.
CJN

counsel participated fully in the application as a party, so did counsel for
the complainant.

[
11
]

CJN
objects
to the disclosure of the information requested by the accused on the grounds
that the information identifies or is likely to identify a journalistic source,
invoking s. 39.1(2) of the
Canadian Evidence Act
[5]

(hereinafter
CEA
). Crown and complainant counsels agree with this
and are also opposing the application for disclosure, adding that it does not
satisfy the criteria set out in s. 278.5.

ISSUES

[
12
]

Can the objection of
CJN
,
third-party record holder, under s. 39.1(2)
CEA
be maintained?

[
13
]

If not, can the application for all records
pertaining to the complainant and her interview with
CJN
in June
2022, be granted?

ANALYSIS

Position of
the parties

[
14
]

Defense counsel argues that the records

are
relevant to issues at trial, namely the complainant’s credibility and the
reliability of her testimony.
[6]

[
15
]

More specifically, he sustains that relevancy goes
to the complainant’s credibility, her motive to fabricate, and collusion with
her sisters.
[7]

He argues the complainant “knowingly lied” to the journalist to bolster her
credibility.
[8]

He contends he needs the records in the possession of

CJN
to
prove this point.

[
16
]

CJN
, Crown and
complainant’s counsels contend that the protection of s. 39.1 of the
CEA

applies to the journalistic source and the journalistic material in possession
of
CJN
regarding the interview given by the complainant.

[
17
]

Subsidiarily, should the Court conclude the
protection of s. 39.1 of the
CEA
does not apply, the adapted
Vice
Media
test set out in
Arsenault
[9]

should apply and the records be considered privileged.

[
18
]

In support of their position against the disclosure
while applying the
Mills
[10]

regime, they also contend the accused has not met his burden to establish
likely relevance of the records themselves. All three argue that the claims
made by the defense that the complainant lied to the journalist, and at the
preliminary inquiry, are unfounded. The same goes for the allegation of
collusion with her sisters. As such, the records

cannot be
relevant to issues at trial.

[
19
]

Moreover, they argue the information requested cannot
be deemed to have significant probative value that is not substantially
outweighed by the danger of prejudice to the proper administration of justice,
as set out by s. 278.92(2)b).

[
20
]

Defense counsel argues that the regime set out in s.
39.1 of the
CEA
cannot be applied as the complainant cannot be
considered a journalistic source. He adds the complainant has no expectation of
privacy over the journalistic material and the
O’connor
[11]
regime should be
applied, as was decided in
R. v. Lim #
4
[12]
.

[
21
]

Subsidiarily, if the Court were to proceed to the
adapted
Vice Media
test, the result would be the same; the
material would not be privileged and should then be disclosed.

Governing
principles

I.

Third party records under s. 278.3

[
22
]

Section 278.3 applications by
an accused are conducted in two stages.

[
23
]

During stage one the accused
must establish
[13]
:

(1) that their application conforms to s. 278.3
(2)-(6);

(2) that the record is “likely relevant”; and

(3) that its production is “necessary in the
interests of justice”.

[
24
]

This last condition requires the trial judge to
inquire, as best as can be done in the absence of having seen the record, into
the “extent to which the record is necessary for the accused to make full answer
and defence”
[14]

and “the probative value of the record”.
[15]

The trial judge is also required to consider any opposing interests that may
justify non-disclosure, such as privacy and equality interests and the
preservation of the integrity of the trial process.
[16]

[
25
]

If the accused does not meet these three
requirements, the application fails.

[
26
]

The threshold of likely relevance provided for in
this regime is higher than that set for the disclosure regime provided for in
R.
v. Stinchcombe
[17]
,
where relevance means "may be useful to the defense".
[18]
However, the threshold of
likely relevance does not constitute an onerous burden. Rather, it requires a
reasonable possibility that the information will have logical probative value
on an issue at trial or as to the competence of a witness to testify.

[
27
]

Evidence is relevant to a fact in issue if it
directly or indirectly makes the existence of that fact more or less likely to
be true.
[19]

For evidence to be relevant, no “minimum probative value” is required
[20]
and the threshold is not
high.
[21]

Relevance is a prerequisite to the admissibility of all evidence offered in a
criminal proceeding.
[22]

[
28
]

Probative value refers to the ability of
evidence to prove or disprove a fact in issue. It is measured by reference to
the significance in the litigation of the fact to which the evidence is
directed, and the ability of that evidence to prove or disprove that fact.
[23]
Since it is a hearing on
admissibility and not concerning the ultimate probative value, probative value,
here, can also be called “probative potential”.

[
29
]

If
an accused meets the stage
one
burden,
the application proceeds to stage two which involves
the review of the records by the trial judge to determine whether to produce the
records to the accused.
[24]

[
30
]

Section 278.7(1) sets out
the pre‑requisites for production of the records to an accused. Again,
“likely relevance” is a prerequisite. Since the judge will have reviewed the
documents before making this second “likely relevance” determination, the
actual contents of the records are now known. Therefore the “likely relevance”
inquiry no longer focuses on what the documents are likely to contain but
focuses instead on whether the known contents could relate to “likely” issues.
[25]

[
31
]

Before ordering production
to the accused, the judge must also be satisfied that production is “necessary
in the interests of justice”. Again, the judge shall consider the salutary and deleterious
effects of the determination on the accused’s right to make a full answer and
defence and on the right to privacy and equality of the complainant or witness,
as the case may be, and any other person to whom the record relates.
[26]

[
32
]

The judge
shall also take the factors specified in
paragraphs 278.5(2)(a) to (h) into account. Once again, this inquiry is
undertaken by applying the same considerations of these reasons, although at
this juncture the determination of whether production is “necessary in the
interests of justice” will be made with the benefit of having seen what the
records contain.
[27]

II.

Section 39.1 of the
Canadian Evidence Act

[
33
]

In 2017, the
Journalistic Source
Protection Act
[28]

was enacted. It amended the
CEA
and the
Criminal Code

to address journalistic source confidentiality and protection of journalistic
related materials.

[
34
]

The amendment to the
CEA
provided
for objections to disclosure of a journalist’s source information. Though not
specifically employing the language of “privilege”, the
CEA

provisions overlap with the Wigmore criteria for case-by-case privilege.
[29]

[
35
]

Section 39.1 of the
CEA
allows a
journalist to object to the disclosure if information or a document on the
grounds that the information or document identifies or is likely to identify a
journalistic source. Once such a claim is maid, the Court must ensure the
information or document is only disclosed in accordance with s. 39.1.
[30]
To make that determination,
the Court must give the parties, and interested persons, a reasonable
opportunity to present observations.
[31]

[
36
]

The two-part test set out in s. 39.1 of the
CEA

for consideration of potential claims of journalistic-confidential source
privilege is the following:

(1)

The Court must determine if the claim of privilege falls within the
criteria set out in s. 39.1. This first part can also be called the threshold
requirements for journalists.

(2)

If the claim falls within the criteria of s. 39.1, the Court must
then determine whether the information or the document should be disclosed in
accordance with the onus and criteria articulated within s. 39.1. This second
part is the disclosure test itself.

[
37
]

At the first part of the test (the threshold
requirements) the journalist asserting the claim of privilege must satisfy two
statutory pre-conditions:

1)

That the individual journalist meets the definition of “journalist”
within s. 39.1; and

2)

That the source satisfies the definition of “journalistic source”
within s. 39.1.
[32]

[
38
]

A journalist is a person whose main occupation
is to contribute directly, either regularly or occasionally, for consideration,
to the collection, writing or production of information for dissemination by
the media, or anyone who assists such a person.
[33]

[
39
]

A journalistic source means a source that
confidentially transmits information to a journalist on the journalist’s
undertaking not to divulge the identity of the source, whose anonymity is
essential to the relationship between the journalist and the source.
[34]

[
40
]

The combined effect of statutory definitions of
journalist and journalistic source serves the same function as the first three
criteria of the Wigmore test.
[35]

[
41
]

John Henry Wigmore was an American jurist and an
expert on law evidence who constructed a test for jurists when trying to
determine if a particular communication is confidential and the factors to be
considered when deciding to protect or compel its disclosure. The theory behind
the Wigmore test is that courts may balance the public interest in maintaining
privilege against the interest the Court may have in pursuing the truth. The
Wigmore criteria are:

1)

The communications must originate in confidence that they will not
be disclosed;

2)

This element of confidentiality must be essential to the full and
satisfactory maintenance of the relationship between the parties;

3)

The relationship must be one which in the opinion of the community
ought to be sedulously fostered; and

4)

The injury to the relationship from the disclosure of the
communications must be greater than the benefit gained from the correct disposal
of the litigation.
[36]

[
42
]

Should an objection fail to satisfy the
threshold requirements set out in s. 39.1(1) of the
CEA
, then its
protection cannot apply.

[
43
]

Once the threshold requirements are met, the
onus shifts to the person seeking disclosure to justify why it should be made.
[37]
Section 39.1(7) sets out the
test for disclosure to be applied to determine if the onus has been met by the
applicant:

a)

The information or the document cannot be
produced in evidence by any other reasonable means; and

b)

The public interest in the determination of justice outweighs the
public interest in preserving confidentiality of the journalistic source,
having regard, to, among other things,

i.

The importance of the information or document to
a central issue in the proceeding,

ii.

Freedom of the press, and

iii.

The impact pf disclosure in the journalistic
source and the journalist.

[
44
]

The first consideration is whether there is any
other reasonable means by which the information being sought can be obtained.
If the person seeking disclosure cannot demonstrate reasonable necessity, the
application must be denied.

[
45
]

If reasonable necessity is demonstrated, the Court
must then carefully balance the criterion of s. 39.1(7)b).

[
46
]

The importance of the information or document to

a
central issue in the proceeding need not be
the
issue in this
proceeding. However, it must be
central
to the proceeding, certainly not
peripheral. Once this has been demonstrated, the Court must consider the
importance of the information to the issue.

[
47
]

The more crucial the information being sought is
to the resolution of a central issue in the proceeding, the more it can be
characterized as important and the more the disclosure will be justified. By
contrast, information that is simply not relevant cannot be characterized as
important.
[38]

[
48
]

As recently underlined again by our Supreme Court
in
Canadian Broadcasting Corp. v. Named Person
[39]
,
freedom of the press plays an important role in Canadian democracy. Indeed,
without free, robust, and independent news media to inform the Canadian public
of what is happening in courtrooms, and in the justice system more broadly,
open justice is of only limited social and democratic utility.
[40]

[
49
]

As noted in
Denis v. Côté
[41]
, this
criterion will quite often weigh against disclosure of a source’s identity. In
fact, mobilizing a journalist against his or her source is incompatible with
freedom of the press and the important mission the media pursues.

[
50
]

However, as Chief Justice Wagner specified in
Denis
v. Côté
, it is possible that an applicant who seeks the disclosure of a
journalistic source’s identity will submit evidence capable of convincing the Court
that the source’s purpose is contrary to the public interest. One such
situation might involve the communication of information the source knows to be
deliberately false for the purpose of hindering the orderly progress of public
business. In such a case, freedom of the press would in the end not have the
same weight in the balancing exercise, because upholding that freedom would
then be incompatible with the very interests it is intended to protect.
[42]

[
51
]

As for the impact of disclosure on the
journalistic source and the journalist, the Court must consider the specific
impact of disclosure on the source and the journalist. This impact can
certainly be imagined in the form of various scenarios without the journalist
having to disclose the information sought. It could take the form of relatively
minor personal or professional inconveniences or more serious professional and
therefore financial consequences, of judicial proceedings, and even of violent
reprisals.
[43]

[
52
]

It is also possible for the Court to consider
other relevant criteria not specifically listed in s. 39.1(7) as they are not
exhaustive.

[
53
]

Finally, balancing is the “heart of the new
statutory scheme”.
[44]

This balancing is a delicate exercise. Disclosure is to be ordered only when
the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. And, if the Court orders disclosure,
it must minimize the disadvantages by imposing conditions that are appropriate
in the circumstances.

III.

The rule of law in Quebec regarding privacy when
dealing with media and open sources: The adapted
Vice Media
test

[
54
]

There is very little case law on the test to be
applied for production of material in the possession of a journalist on the
application of an accused, as opposed to such records sought by the state.

[
55
]

Defense counsels argues
R. v Lim #4
,
applying the
O’Connor
regime, should inspire the Court to
distinguish this case from the Superior Court decision in
R. v. Arsenault
[45]

which

sets out the applicable framework for disclosure of journalistic
material when dealing with privacy concerns in matters where the media obtained
its information from open sources rather than anonymous ones.

[
56
]

As Justice Moldaver pointed out in
Vice Media
inc
.
[46]
,
the enactment of s. 39.1 of the
CAE
serves as a further
illustration of the important distinction between confidential and
non-confidential sources
[47]

and that the distinction between confidential and non-confidential sources
should not be erased.
[48]

[
57
]

Context is crucial, and it should not be assumed
that the existence or absence of a confidentiality agreement makes no
difference in the analysis.
[49]

[
58
]

In fact, the absence of a confidentiality agreement
does not give the state, nor the accused, free rein to compel production of
materials in the hands of the media.
[50]

Even where the source of the information sought is non-confidential, compelled
production may cause chilling effects, and the impact on the media and the
privacy interests at stake may nonetheless be significant.
[51]

[
59
]

Moreover, a journalist's right to confidentiality
in the process of collecting and disseminating information is a right to
confidentiality distinct from that of his or her sources.
[52]
A communication order will
have the same consequences on the journalist and on his or her right to
confidentiality in the collection and dissemination of information as well as
on the sources, regardless of whether the request comes from the state or the
accused.
[53]

[
60
]

As outlined by Justice Bourque in
R. v.

Arsenault
, the distinction between a request from the state and that
from the accused under the
Mills
regime is of little importance
since the request is covered by s. 8 of the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedom
.
[54]

Thus, the right of the media to the protection of s. 8 applies both to a request
for the issuance of a search warrant from the state and to a request for a
production order from the accused issued under the
Mills
or
O'Connor

regime.

[
61
]

After reviewing the significance of amendments
to the
Criminal code
, Justice Bourque states that a distinct right to
confidentiality exists for journalists, independently of their sources.
[55]
This right is of a
constitutional nature as it stems directly from
s. 2b)
of the
Canadian
Charter
of Freedom and Rights.
[56]

[
62
]

Whether forced disclosure is requested by the
police or by the accused, the analysis is the same and the potential hazards
for freedom of the press remain equally perilous.
[57]

[
63
]

It is through a meticulous examination of the
applicable case law, combined with the paradigm shift brought about by the
enactment of s. 39.1 of the
CEA
, that Justice Bourque adapts the
Vice
Media
common law regime to requests for a communication order in
relation to the media from a party other than the state.

[
64
]

She concludes that this adapted version of the
Vice
Media
regime respects both legislative and jurisprudential developments
and reflects the new paradigm recognized by the Supreme Court when it comes to
such orders.
[58]

[
65
]

Essentially, when deciding on an application
seeking to obtain journalistic material emanating from an open source, the Court
must:

1)

Ensure that the media outlet has been notified;

2)

Ensure respect of the preliminary procedural requirements (as an
example,
s. 278.3
of the
Criminal Code
);

3)

Proceed to balancing the opposing societal imperatives; and

4)

Impose conditions to mitigate the prejudicial
impacts of the projected disclosure order.
[59]

[
66
]

The principal societal imperatives that are at
play during the balancing stage are adapted by Justice Bourque, from those
prescribed by Justice Moldaver in
Vice Media Inc
[60]
,
to
address claims made by an accused rather than by the state. They are the
following:

a)

The likelihood and extent of any potential chilling effects;

b)

The scope the material sought and whether the
order is narrowly tailored;

c)

The likely probative value of the materials
;

d)

Whether there are alternative sources from which
the information may reasonably be obtained and, if so, whether the applicant
has made all reasonable efforts to obtain the information from these sources;

e)

The effect of the prior partial publication, now
assessed on a case-by-case basis;

f)

The vital role that the media plays in the functioning of a
democratic society
; and the fact that the media
will generally be an innocent third party; and

g)

The nature of the sought documents
[61]

[
67
]

Of course, the
stare decisis
doctrine
applying to the
Arsenault
decision, the Court is bound by it.

IV.

Victim’s rights considerations

[
68
]

In the hopes of redressing past injustices, the
rights to privacy and psychological security of victims of crime have been
explicitly protected in their own instrument, the
Canadian Victims Bill
of Rights
[62]

(herein after the
CVBR
).

[
69
]

Bestowed with quasi-constitutional status, the
CVBR

imposes that federal legislation, like the
Criminal Code
and the
CEA
,
be applied in compliance with the statute and it’s enumerated rights.
[63]

[
70
]

The preamble of the
CVBR
affirms
the importance of recognizing courtesy, compassion, and respect for the dignity
of the victims as priorities throughout the criminal justice system. These
values must guide litigants and deciders when navigating evidentiary provisions
such as
s. 278.1
-
278.9
of the
Criminal Code
. Just like these provisions have
been enacted to protect the privacy and dignity of complainants and witnesses
in sexual assaults procedures, the
CVBR
serves as a beacon of the
society’s concern for the fair treatment of vulnerable persons who have been historically
wronged by a merciless and overly legalistic justice system.
[64]

[
71
]

As Justice Cutler calls attention to in
R.
v Roland
, « Parliament and the courts have recognized the disadvantaged
position complainants in sexual assault prosecutions and have taken steps to
address the often irrelevant and unfair attacks on the character, privacy, and
security of the complainants. »
[65]

[
72
]

As underlined in the decision concerning Pre-Trial
Application A, our Supreme Court acknowledged again the history of myths and
stereotypes against complainants in its recent decision
R. v. Kruk
.
[66]
It reminds us
about the unique history and specific remedial purpose of the prohibition
against myths and stereotypes that undermine the credibility of sexual assault
complainants : to remove discriminatory legal rules that contributed to the
view that women, as a group, were less worthy of belief and did not deserve
legal protection against sexual violence.
[67]

[
73
]

Hence, the Court must be mindful of the treatment
victims have suffered in the past so as not to allow or perpetuate behavior
that supports mistreatment of their character or dignity. This, while bearing
in mind the objectives of protecting the integrity of the trial, the accused’s
trial rights, the security and privacy of complainants, and equality rights.
[68]

[
74
]

It is with these principles in mind that the Court
must now determine if the objection of the third-party record holder, a news
organization, can be maintained. If not, the Court will determine if the accused’s
application can be granted.

Application
to case at bar

I.

General remarks concerning the application itself

[
75
]

Though the identity of the person giving the
information in the Podcast and the news articles is protected by not showing an
image, blurring their voice, and refraining from giving specific information to
identify this person, this person is indeed identified as the complainant by
the journalist.

[
76
]

All the evidence tendered leads to the following
logical and reasonable inference; this person is the complainant in the present
case and her identity is protected by the journalist. This an important and
established premise with which the Court will analyze Pre-Trial application B.
[69]

[
77
]

Here, defense submits Pre-trial Application B under
the
Mills
regime, as
s. 278.3
provides.

[
78
]

It is only following
CJN’
s objection
under s. 39.1 of the
CEA
that defense argues the complainant has
no expectation of privacy in the information and/or documents he seeks to
obtain.

[
79
]

When replying to oral arguments presented by Crown,
complainant and
CJN
counsels, defense counsel explains that this
is the reason the scope of his motion is so wide, asking for the disclosure of
the copy of all recorded interviews given by the complainant to
CJN
,
copy of all written exchanges between the journalist and the complainant, copy
off all the notes taken by the journalist during her meetings with the
complainant and copy of all the materials provided by the complainant to
CJN

and its journalist un support of her claims.
[70]

[
80
]

When filing Pre-Trial application B, defense specifically
referred to the
Mills

regime and
s. 278.1
-278.91 as the
applicable framework.
[71]

[
81
]

As such, when defense now argues the complainant
has no expectation of privacy in the records held by
CJN
, the Court
underlines that this is not what Pre-Trial application B says. On the contrary,
the term “record” is used in paragraphs 73, 77 and 83 of the application when
referring to the information in possession of the journalist. And, when
addressing the expectation of privacy of the complainant, paragraph 84
indicates she has little expectation of privacy, not that she has none.

II.

Erroneous allegations in the application

[
82
]

As for the application itself, it contains many allegations
unsupported by the evidence tendered.

a)

Recordings

[
83
]

III.

Objection by
CJN
following s. 39.1 of
the
CEA

[
141
]

Defense argues about the fact that the regime set
out in s. 39.1 of the
CEA
cannot apply because
CJN

did not file an affidavit supporting its claim and the promise of
confidentiality by its journalist to the person being interviewed.

[
142
]

Indeed, although an affidavit by its journalist was
initially anounced by counsel for
CJN
, it was not filed into
evidence. Consequently, the Court cannot, and will not, rely on any argument
referring to this affidavit.

[
143
]

Nowhere in the
CEA
or in case law
examined is there a requirement for such an affidavit. Hence, the Court is of
the opinion that such affidavit is not required if the evidence otherwise
establishes that the regime applies.

[
144
]

Nevertheless, it is the burden of the journalist
invoking the protection of s. 39.1 of the
CEA
to satisfy the
threshold requirements for the regime to apply which need to be established on the
balance of probabilities.

[
145
]

The evidence tendered does fulfill the requirement
concerning the journalist,
CJN
journalist Ellin Bessner being such
a person.

[
146
]

It is the definition of journalistic source that
poses a challenge here. The statute is clear when it says it is a source that
confidentially transmits information to a journalist on the journalist’s
undertaking

not to divulge the identity of the source, whose anonymity is essential to the
relationship between the journalist and the source (The Court underlines).

[
147
]

In the French version, it is defined in the
following manner : « source qui transmet confidentiellement de l’information à
un journaliste
avec son engagement, en contrepartie,
de ne pas divulguer
l’identité de la source, dont l’anonymat est essentiel aux rapports entre le
journaliste et la source (The Court underlines). The
French word “contrepartie” is used, meaning “in exchange of”, or “compensated
by”.

[
148
]

The terms “confidentially”, “identity” and
“anonymity” are not defined at s. 39.1 of the
CEA
. To enlighten
us, we can turn to the common meaning of these terms, which are defined as
follows
[89]
:

•

“confidentially”: in a way that is intended to be
private or secret; privately.

•

“identity”: who or what a person or thing is.

•

“anonymity”: the fact or condition of being
nameless or unidentified.

[
149
]

“Secrecy” is therefore at the heart of
communications between a journalist and his or her source. Confiding in a
journalist, under the cover of anonymity, can take several forms, as long as
the journalist is careful not to reveal the identity of the person.

[
150
]

As Justice Bourque pointed out
in
Arsenault
,
society expects that when a source, complainant or not, in a sexual assault
case confides in a journalist, that his or her confidences will not be
disclosed beyond what the journalist considers necessary and useful for the
purposes of reporting his or her work.
[90]
It
also expects the journalist to protect the confidentiality of his or her
investigative file, particularly in a case as sensitive and delicate as one of
sexual assault by a rabbi [...] in this specific Jewish community.

[
151
]

Justice Bourque also made a particular point of
distinguishing between sources, complainants and journalists when detailing
their privacy interest.

[
152
]

When specifically addressing complainant’s
interest in protecting their right to privacy while exchanging with a
journalist, she said it was “undeniable”, that their story belongs to them,
that they must be able to choose why, when, how and to
whom they entrust it, without fear of opening the door to an automatic invasion
of their private life because the state has decided to bring criminal charges.
[91]

[
153
]

When referring to the journalistic sources’
privacy interests, she stated that they were “amply demonstrated” by the
evidence tendered through the reporter’s sworn affidavit.
[92]

[
154
]

This specific distinction by Justice Bourque between
complainant’s and journalistic sources in the protection of their privacy
interests allows this Court to consider the “undeniable” interest the
complainant had in protecting her right to privacy while exchanging with the
CJN

journalist. She was entrusting the journalist with her story. And, when her
story was published, different measures were taken to protect her identity.
That being said, the Court is unable to conclude, on the evidence tendered and
on the balance of probabilities, if the complainant did so in exchange for anonymity.

[
155
]

As for the reference to a Court ordered
publication ban of the identity of the complainant by the journalist, it does
not, in itself, allow for the protection of s. 39.1 to apply.

[
156
]

Nonetheless, it is important to mention that such
publication bans enable victims and witnesses, and others, to participate in the
criminal justice system without suffering the negative consequences of being
publicly identified. A victim, witness, or justice system participant may
decide that they no longer wish to be the subject of a publication ban or they
may wish to have certain conditions modified.
[93]

To this day, the publication ban in the present case is still in force.

[
157
]

Here, the references by the
CJN
journalist
to the Court ordered publication ban rather serve as confirmation that she has
committed herself to not disclose the identity of her source. Hence, the source
here is not an open source, as was the case for some of the sources in the
Arsenault

case. However, this doesn’t resolve the issue of an undertaking by the
journalist to preserve the anonymity of the complainant in exchange for the
information shared.

[
158
]

On the other hand, a person who chooses to
participate in an interview, to answer a journalist's questions, with their
face uncovered or name mentioned, is a revealing indicator of the absence of
"secret", of "confidentiality”, in communications and, of the
absence of anonymity. This was in fact the case concerning three sources in

Arsenault
that were then considered to be open sources.
[94]

[
159
]

Here, many elements are present in the evidence
regarding confidentiality of the identity of the source, namely the blurring of
her voice, the absence of any image to identify her, the use of “they” pronouns
and, finally, the referral to the Court ordered publication ban. But, nowhere
in the evidence is there something to support the inference that the person
transmitting the information required anonymity to do so or that the journalist
promised her anonymity for her to do so.

[
160
]

It is tempting, because of the different measures
taken by the journalist to ensure the protection of the identity of the source
(here, the complainant), to infer the journalist promised this person not to
divulge her identity in exchange for the information shared.

[
161
]

But the measures themselves only prove that the
journalist did in fact protect the complainant’s identity, but not especially
on the undertaking to do so in exchange for the information shared.  Here, the
evidence does not allow the court to conclude that the journalist did so
because

of an undertaking in exchange for the confidential transmission of information.
As an example, the complainant might have said she did not mind her identity
being known but the journalist no willing to let it be known because of the
Court ordered publication ban.

[
162
]

Let’s not forget the combined effect of statutory
definitions of journalist and journalistic source serves the same function as
the first three criteria of the Wigmore test at common law.
[95]
In fact, the promise of
confidentiality must be
explicitly
made.
[96]
Here, the evidence does not
support such a conclusion on the balance of probabilities.

[
163
]

Consequently, the threshold requirements are not
met as the person transmitting the information cannot be deemed a journalistic
source, as defined by s. 39.1 of the
CEA
.

[
164
]

If the Court errs in this conclusion, and the s.
39.1 of the
CEA
regime should apply, it’s important to underline
that defense would not satisfy its burden to demonstrate that the information
or the document in the possession of
CJN
cannot be produced in
evidence by any other reasonable means namely because the allegations made by
defense are unsupported by the evidence. The Court concludes there is no
evidence that can be made by obtaining the journalistic material in possession
of
CJN
.

[
165
]

Moreover, the defense disposes of several means to
attack the complainant’s version and/or intentions. This can be done by
cross-examination of the complainant at trial (even referring to the
preliminary transcripts) compelling other civilian witnesses to testify, and
adducing statements emanating from the Crown disclosure.

[
166
]

But, even if reasonable necessity was demonstrated,
the public interest in the determination of justice does
not outweigh the public interest in preserving confidentiality of the
journalistic source, namely because the information requested has no importance
to a central issue at trial.

[
167
]

Certainly, the defense can argue that
credibility is a central issue at trial. However, considering the conclusion of
the Court that the application’s allegations are unsupported by the evidence
tendered, then there is nothing in the information requested that could be even
remotely useful to attack the credibility of the complainant at trial.

[
168
]

Additionally, freedom of the press is in itself an
important component of our democracy. Recent times have shown us the significant
role the media plays in shedding light on sexual assaults. These are crimes
that are mostly committed in secrecy, towards vulnerable persons who generally
fear denouncing their abuser, dreading the consequences they may have to bear
if they do so. This certainly seems to be the case in the particular Jewish
Community described in the news articles. And, for victims to have a safe place
in the media where they can confide, and maybe even seek to find other persons
like themselves, who might be victims also, is not to be discouraged by forced
disclosure.

[
169
]

Consequently, if the protection at s. 39.1 of the
CEA

had applied, and even if defense had satisfied the first criteria of the
disclosure test set out at s. 39.1 of the
CEA,
the application
would be denied at the balancing stage.

[
170
]

The Court will now analyse
CJN
’s objection
following the adapted
Vice Media
regime.

IV.

Objection by
CJN
under the adapted

Vice Media
test in
Arsenault

[
171
]

As was done in
Arsenault
, to adapt
the
Vice Media
regime to accused’s application, the analysis must
be carried out by replacing at each stage of the analysis the state's interest
in investigating crimes and prosecuting their perpetrators with the right of
the accused to full answer and defense.

Step 1: Notice to the Media concerned by the application

[
172
]

Here,
CJN
is the media concerned
by the application. It has received notice from the accused of it’s
s. 278.3
application.

Step 2: Compliance with the legal prerequisites.

[
173
]

The application is presented under the
Mills

regime which requires likely relevance to be satisfied for such an application
to succeed at the first stage to order production for review by the judge.

[
174
]

As the Supreme Court reminds us in
Mills
:

Parliament also
sought to recognize the prevalence of sexual violence against women and
children and its disadvantageous impact on their rights, to encourage the
reporting of incidents of sexual violence, to recognize the impact of the
production of personal information on the efficacy of treatment, and to
reconcile fairness to complainants with the rights of the accused. […]
Parliament
may also be understood to be recognizing “horizontal” equality concerns
,
where women’s inequality results from the acts of other individuals and groups
rather than the state, but which nonetheless may have many consequences for the
criminal justice system.
[97]

(The Court underlines)

[
175
]

Combined with the
CVBR
provisions,
horizontal equality concerns may serve as guidelines when examining likely
relevancy under the
Mills
regime.

[
176
]

Of course, qualifying the information as likely
relevant to the question of credibility of the complainant is insufficient
since the
Mills
regime provides that the mere fact that the
information exists, or that it relates to the event which is the subject of the
trial or that it could relate to the credibility of the complainant or a
witness, are all insufficient to justify disclosure at stage one of the motion,
therefore to the judge for review.

[
177
]

The fact that credibility will be a central issue at trial is not in
question here. However, attributing significance to all the complainant’s prior
statements, in this case, to a journalist to which she did not give details
about the sexual assault except to state how old she was when it happened, is
problematic. Indeed, it is an assertion that is at odds with the evolution of
legislation and case law regarding the prosecution of sexual offenses.
[98]

[
178
]

There is no doubt that the right to
cross-examination is one of the important facets of the public interest in the
administration of justice.
[99]

That being said, seeking to challenge the credibility of a complainant is not a
limitless venture and it is not exempted from judicial scrutiny.

[
179
]

Summarily, defense argues the only way it will be
able to test the complainant’s credibility is to cross-examine her on other
matters (namely the ones dealt with in her interview with
CJN
)
arguing this is especially important since she does not recall a lot of things
about the sexual assault itself.

[
180
]

The Court cannot agree with this argument as it
would mean any prior statement made by the complainant would be open to be
addressed without likely relevance being established.

[
181
]

Of course, defense submits the likely relevance
threshold has been met. The Court disagrees.

[
182
]

It is impossible, while relying on the evidence
tendered, to give any value to defense allegations that the complainant lied,
or “knowingly lied, when talking to the police, the journalist or while
testifying at the preliminary inquiry. Contending that she lied with
unsupported allegations is futile. The same goes for what defense calls
collusion or motive to fabricate so the complainant would be believed when
stating she is a victim of sexual assault by the accused.

[
183
]

As detailed earlier in the section concerning
erroneous allegations in the application presented by the accused, the Court
can only conclude that defense is arguing allegations that are unsupported by
the evidence. This also applies to oral arguments presented in support of the application,
in particular the evolving argument concerning a recording of a phone call by
the complainant.

[
184
]

Additionally, time and manner of contact between
the complainant and
CJN
are irrelevant to the matter at hand. It
certainly would not sustain the defense’s argument that the complainant “knowingly
lied” about a past victim of the accused or that she lied about being a victim
herself.

[
185
]

The fact that the accused does not seek to obtain
records from
CBC,
to obtain time and manner of contact between
the complainant and its journalist, demonstrates even more the irrelevance of
such a request concerning the records of
CJN
journalist.

[
186
]

Furthermore, and as
CJN
counsel drew
attention to at the hearing, the Podcast and news articles are much more about
sexual abuse in the Jewish Community than the sexual abuse allegedly committed
by the accused, as little information is shared by the journalist about the actual
case itself.
[100]

[
187
]

The complainant testified at the preliminary
inquiry that she did not reach out to
CJN.
[101]
“Reaching out”
can be interpreted as making contact or making an effort in communicating with
someone. It doesn’t necessarily mean the complainant would never have contacted

CJN
about making an interview. For instance, it could mean a
third party put them in contact.

[
188
]

Moreover, the mere fact that a complainant said
something about a matter which could be the subject of cross-examination at
trial, does not raise a reasonable possibility that the complainant's statement
will have some probative value in the assessment of her credibility.
[102]

[
189
]

Here, there is no basis for concluding that the
records have some potential to provide the accused with some added information
not already available to the defense or have some potential impeachment value.
[103]

[
190
]

Ultimately, and as was outlined earlier in this
decision, the information upon which the accused relies to obtain disclosure of
confidential records are either erroneous, misleading, or purely hypothetical.

[
191
]

In conclusion, the application does not meet the
conditions of
s. 278.5
of the
Criminal Code
, the evidence being insufficient to
demonstrate likely relevance.

[
192
]

This conclusion is sufficient to dispose of the application
and objection to disclosure by
CJN
.

[
193
]

However, if the Court errs on this question and
given the importance and diversity of interests at stake, it will continue the
analysis of the application under the adapted
Vice Media
regime.

Step 3: Balancing exercise

a)

the likelihood and extent of any potential
chilling effects

[
194
]

Even if the potential chilling effect can be less
important for open sources, it is still important to consider the context to
examine this first criterion.

[
195
]

Journalists and journalism suffer from a “chilling
effect” when sources are afraid to speak for fear that their identity or their
communications might be revealed and journalists are worried, that they may be
compelled to reveal the identities of their sources, and the content of their
communications, to the authorities. Ultimately, forced disclosure might
discourage sources from speaking out and journalists from accomplishing their
important role in our democracy of informing society.

[
196
]

Here, we learn from the evidence tendered that the
community in which the accused was living in is “very extremist”.
[104]
This is explained by the
executive director of
Magen
, Shana Aaronson.
Magen for communities

is a group that works with survivors of sexual abuse in Israel. Shana Aaronson
is working with several survivors who allege they are also victims of the
accused, though none have made official complaints to Israel police, yet. She
explains, in Ellin Bessner’s news article, that this is not surprising since
this extremist community is known for not trusting the police. She adds: “Quite
the opposite. This is the kind of community where they believe the police are
Nazis.”

[
197
]

We also learn of
Za’akah organization
in New
Jersey, which advocates for victims of childhood sexual abuse in the Jewish
Community. Both Ariella Kay and Asher Lovy of
Za’akah
participate to the
news article written by Ellin Bessner. They explain that, traditionally,
victims who do come forward either to their rabbis or, in rare cases, to law
enforcement, suffer tremendous personal backlash.
Za’akah
has heard of
victims shunned by the Jewish Community, but who also lose access to housing
and job opportunities, and even marriage prospects. There are also people who
face extreme ostracism.
[105]

[
198
]

In this particular context, revealed by the
evidence tendered, the Court could certainly fear for the complainant, and the
journalist herself, if the journalistic material was to be disclosed. And the
fact that the complainant said in the Podcast that she did not fear “backlash”
does not diminish the possibility that she might suffer consequences from
forced disclosure. The same can be said about the journalist and any other potential
victim who might want to confide to a journalist, or might already have done
so, in such a manner.

[
199
]

Finally, as underlined by Justice Bourque in
Arsenault
,
ordering a journalist to hand over unpublished material sends the message to
the population that the journalist has no real independence.
[106]

[
200
]

This criterion advocates for non-disclosure.

b)

the scope the material sought and whether the order is narrowly
tailored

[
201
]

The scope of the material covered by the
application is extremely wide.

[
202
]

In fact, defense argues that it may reach as far
since the complainant has no expectation of privacy in the material.

[
203
]

Though oral arguments supporting defense
application mostly pertain to a recording, the exchanges the complainant would
have had concerning a past victim of the accused and the dates at which she
would have communicated with
CJN
journalist, the conclusions of
Pre-Trial Application B are not limited to these records but refer to basically
everything the journalist should have in her possession about this interview.

[
204
]

As argued by
CJN
counsel, to which
counsels for Crown and complainant agree, the request is a thinly veiled fishing
expedition.
[107]

[
205
]

This criterion advocates for non-disclosure.

c)

the likely probative value of the materials

[
206
]

As stated earlier while analyzing the erroneous
allegations in the application and likely relevance when addressing the compliance
with the
s. 278.5
prerequisites, there is no likely probative value to the
materials requested.

[
207
]

This criterion advocates for non-disclosure.

d)

whether there are alternative sources from which
the information may reasonably be obtained and, if so, whether the accused has
made all reasonable efforts to obtain the information from these sources

[
208
]

Defense counsel argues he needs the journalistic
material to prove the complainant is lying or “knowingly lying”. One point he
wants to make is that the complainant lied about facts that do not pertain to
the sexual assault charge with which the accused is charged, hence she cannot
be trusted. Another one is that she lied to bolster her claim of being sexually
assaulted.

[
209
]

The Court has already decided the evidence does
not establish the complainant lied or “knowingly lied”. Additionally, assuming
she did lie is contrary to the objectives pursued by the
Mills

regime and evolution of case law concerning myths and stereotype looking to
eradicate that victims of sexual assault lie or make contradictory statements.
[108]
It would also undermine the
truth-seeking function of the trial.
[109]

[
210
]

This criterion advocates for non-disclosure.

e)

the effect of the prior partial publication, now
assessed on a case-by-case basis

[
211
]

In this case, it’s impossible to know if some of
the journalistic material given by the complainant was not broadcasted by the
journalist.

[
212
]

This makes it also impossible to determine the
extent to which the published material differs (if it does) from the entire
record in possession of the journalist.

[
213
]

Prior partial publication then has no impact on
the question of disclosure of the records to the accused.

[
214
]

This criterion cannot advocate for disclosure.

f)

the vital role that the media plays in the
functioning of a democratic society and the fact that the media will generally
be an innocent third party

[
215
]

From traditional platforms such as television,
radio, and newspapers to modern digital media outlet (such as social media), media
has become an integrated part our society, present in our daily lives and contributing
to shaping societal norms.

[
216
]

One of the primary functions of the media is to
provide information to the public. Media also acts as a powerful medium
for the expression of public opinion and the functioning of a democratic
society.  In fact, in democratic societies, media acts as a watchdog,
ensuring transparency, exposing corruption, and safeguarding the principles of
democracy.

[
217
]

Media can also raise awareness about social
issues, promoting dialogue and driving change in our society. It can also shed
light on matters such as human rights, environmental concerns, and
discrimination. By the media, these realities are put to the public who can
then form an opinion about them. Hence, media can shape public perception and consciousness.

[
218
]

Through investigative journalism, media can
mobilize attention and support for different causes. When giving a voice to vulnerable
persons and communities, media can play a pivotal role in advocating social
justice and tending to a more tolerant and inclusive society.

[
219
]

More recently, media has played an important
role in advocating for sexual abuse victim’s rights by exposing criminal
behavior they have had to deal with and suffer through.

[
220
]

In summary, a healthy democracy requires an
informed public. To inform the public, journalists depend on their ability to
protect their sources’ confidentiality and the journalistic material gathered
through them.

[
221
]

In this case, the evidence exposes a reality
that is problematic for victims emanating from this particular Jewish
community. This adds an additional layer to the role of the media, particularly
in this Jewish Community.

[
222
]

As outlined earlier in this decision, executive
director of
Magen
, Shana Aaronson, says to
CJN
that she is
currently working with several survivors who allege they are also victims of the
accused, but have not made official complaints.
[110]

[
223
]

In such a context, the media’s role is of a
particular importance.

[
224
]

This criterion advocates for non-disclosure.

g)

the nature of the documents sought

[
225
]

Prudence is of the upmost importance here as the
information sought pertains mostly to information gathered because the
complainant was sexually assaulted [...], a rabbi in their Jewish community,
when she was 7 or 8 years old.

[
226
]

The records sought pertain to the complainant’s
identity as a sexual abuse victim when she was a child and her desire to compel
other victims to come forward.

[
227
]

Again, as detailed in the decision concerning Pre-Trial
application A, it
is perfectly legitimate for a victim
of unwanted sexual touching to be angry with their attacker and to express
their frustrations with the legal process, especially if this person was a
child victim of a trusted [...]. Speaking about it publicly can certainly have
a therapeutic effect and even encourage other victims to take action – a worthy
goal.
[111]

[
228
]

The simple act of sharing such information can
be detrimental to the complainant
[112]

and any other who might want to act in the same manner. Again, this is possible
even if the complainant states in the interview that she does not fear backlash
from her community. Considering the
CVBR
, the Court has the duty
to respect the complainant’s dignity, and others like her.

[
229
]

This criterion advocates for non-disclosure.

Step 4: Impose conditions to mitigate the prejudicial impacts of the
projected disclosure order

[
230
]

This step is irrelevant in the case at bar.

CONCLUSION

[
231
]

The Court
finds the accused did not satisfy the criteria set out in

s. 278.5
concerning all material requested in Pre-Trial Application B, namely
the likely relevance prerequisite.

[
232
]

CJN
’s objection to Pre-Trial Application B under s.
39.1 of the
CEA
is rejected as the journalist did not establish
that
the person transmitting the information is a
journalistic
source
as defined by s. 39.1 of the
CEA
.

[
233
]

If the person had been considered a
journalistic
source
, the defense would not have satisfied its burden to establish that the
information requested cannot be produced in evidence by any other reasonable
means
, nor that t
he public interest in the determination of justice outweighs the
public interest in preserving confidentiality of the journalistic source.

[
234
]

CJN
’s objection to Pre-Trial Application B under
the adapted
Vice Media
regime is maintained as the material
requested by the accused is privileged and cannot be disclosed.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT

[
235
]

REJECTS
CJN
’s objection under s. 39.1 of the
CEA
;

[
236
]

MAINTAINS
CJN
’s objection under the adapted
Vice Media
test;

[
237
]

DECLARES
privileged all information communicated to
CJN

in any way whatsoever, by the source in the Podcast and news articles of [...],
2022;

[
238
]
